pronunciation.t: Letters stack into syllable blocks: 가 = ga
pronunciation.tip: ㄱ (g) + ㅏ (a) stack into 가. Every block = one syllable: 한국 (han-guk) = Korea!

pronunciation.t: ㅇ is silent at the start, NG at the end
pronunciation.tip: 아 (a) starts silent; 방 (bang) ends NG. Same letter, two jobs!

pronunciation.t: Double consonants are tense: 까 vs 가
pronunciation.tip: 까다롭다 vs 가다 — tense sounds pop! 눈 (eye) vs 눈 (snow)? Same — context saves you!
낮 (day) ends like 't'. Don't release the final sound — hold it!
가요 (I go, polite). Drop 요 only with close friends. When unsure — always 요!

alphabet.title: Hangul: 14 consonants + 10 vowels
alphabet.explain: Hangul is the world's most scientific alphabet — designed in 1443! Consonants show tongue shapes, vowels show heaven (•), earth (ㅡ) and humans (ㅣ). Combine into blocks: 한 + 글 = 한글!

counting.title: Counting: native + sino systems
counting.explain: Korean has TWO number systems! NATIVE (하나, 둘, 셋) counts things, age, hours. SINO (일, 이, 삼) counts money, minutes, dates. Learn both — natives switch constantly!
rules: Things/age/hours = NATIVE (하나, 둘). Money/minutes/dates = SINO (일, 이).
Sino 11+ stacks: 십일 = 10-1, 이십 = 2-10s. Native 20+ needs new words (스물 = 20)!

grammar.title: 저는X입니다 + 만나서 반갑습니다
grammar.explain: 저는 미나입니다 = I am Mina. 는/은 marks the topic, 입니다 ends formally. 만나서 반갑습니다 = meeting-you-is-joy!

lessons.title: 숫자와 전화번호
lessons.learn: Native numbers 하나·둘·셋 count things and tell age; before a counter 둘 becomes 두 and 셋 becomes 세. Phone numbers are read one digit at a time, and zero is 공, never 영.

grammar.title: Native numbers and counters
grammar.pattern: 하나 · 둘 · 셋 → 한 개 · 두 개 · 세 개 · 전화번호가 뭐예요? · 공일공
grammar.explain: Sino-Korean numbers (일 이 삼) do dates, money and minutes; native numbers do counting and age. Before a counter the last two shapes shorten: 둘 to 두, 셋 to 세. In a phone number each digit stands alone, so the counter rule does not apply at all.

mistakes.why: 둘 shortens to 두 before the counter 개.
A telephone zero is read 공; 영 is the number zero in arithmetic.

lessons.title: Counters: 개 and 명
lessons.learn: Count things with NATIVE numbers + 개! 사과 세 개 (3 apples), 책 한 개 (1 book — 하나→한!). People: 명! 학생 두 명 (2 students). 몇 개예요? = How many?

grammar.title: Native + 개/명
grammar.explain: Before counters, numbers shorten: 하나→한 개, 둘→두 개, 셋→세 개, 넷→네 개! 사과 세 개 주세요 = Three apples, please! 몇 개예요? = How many?

lessons.title: 가족이 있어요
lessons.learn: Family words carry the speaker's position: a woman says 언니 or 오빠 where a man says 누나 or 형, and a younger sibling is 동생 to everyone. Existence takes 있어요, and the thing that exists takes 이/가, not 을/를.

grammar.title: 있어요 and 없어요
grammar.pattern: 저는 동생이 있어요 · 동생이 없어요 · 어머니가 계세요
grammar.explain: Having and being there are the same verb in Korean: 있다. The thing that exists takes 이/가. For a living person older or higher than you the honorific 계시다 replaces 있다, which is why the question 어머니가 계세요? is polite and 어머니가 있어요? is blunt.

examples.en: There are four of us in my family.

mistakes.why: 있다 takes 이/가 on what exists, never 을/를.

lessons.title: 아요/어요 verbs: 먹어요
lessons.learn: Verbs end 아요/어요! 먹어요 (I eat), 마셔요 (I drink). Negative: 안 먹어요 (don't eat). Past: 먹었어요 (ate)! Same for I/you/he — NO conjugation! Time words do the work!

grammar.title: 어요/아요 · 안 · 었어요
grammar.explain: 먹어요 (eat), 안 먹어요 (don't eat), 먹었어요 (ate), 안 먹었어요 (didn't eat). 아-stems take 아요 (살아요), others 어요 (먹어요)!
mistakes: Saying 먹아요 for 먹다 — ㅓ-stems take 어요!
Saying 안 먹어요 for past — past: 안 먹었어요!

lessons.title: 카페에서 주문해요
lessons.learn: Ordering is one frame: the item, the counter, then 주세요. Drinks take the counter 잔 and hot and cold are adjectives placed before the noun, 뜨거운 커피 and 차가운 커피.

grammar.title: Ordering with 주세요
grammar.pattern: 커피 한 잔 주세요 · 아메리카노 두 잔 주세요 · 뜨거운 걸로 주세요
grammar.explain: 주세요 is the polite request built on 주다. The order is noun, counter, then 주세요; the choice between two things takes -(으)로, as in 뜨거운 걸로 주세요 — the hot one, please.

mistakes.why: A drink is counted in 잔; 개 counts objects.
Korean puts the object before the verb.

culture.text: Hangul 한글 is the only widely used writing system with a recorded birthday: King Sejong promulgated it in 1443, and its 14 consonants and 10 vowels are drawn to match the shape of the mouth that makes them. Because it is that regular, a learner can read Korean aloud in an afternoon. Politeness is built into the grammar, not just the tone: 안녕하세요 means be at peace, and 저는 …입니다 states who you are without ever saying I am as a separate verb.

reading.text: 저는 미나입니다. 서울에 삽니다. 아침에 커피를 마시고 학교에 갑니다. 한국어를 공부합니다. 선생님은 친절합니다. 오후에는 친구를 만납니다. 친구는 학생입니다. 우리는 같이 밥을 먹습니다. 저녁에는 집에서 쉽니다. 주말에는 친구와 시장에 갑니다. 과일과 빵을 삽니다. 그리고 커피를 마시면서 이야기를 합니다. 밤에는 한국 드라마를 보고 일기를 씁니다. 조금 힘들지만 재미있습니다.
reading.gloss: I am Mina. I live in Seoul. In the morning I drink coffee and go to school. I study Korean. The teacher is kind. In the afternoon I meet a friend. My friend is a student. We eat together. In the evening I rest at home. At the weekend I go to the market with a friend. We buy fruit and bread. And we drink coffee and talk. At night I watch Korean dramas and write a diary. It is a little hard, but it is fun.

listening.script:
미나: 안녕하세요.
지훈: 안녕하세요. 처음 뵙겠습니다. 저는 지훈입니다.
미나: 반갑습니다. 저는 미나입니다.
지훈: 미나 씨, 한국어를 공부하십니까?
미나: 네, 조금 공부합니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
listening.gloss: Mina: Hello. Jihun: Hello. How do you do, I am Jihun. Mina: Nice to meet you, I am Mina. Jihun: Mina, do you study Korean? Mina: Yes, a little. Please treat me well.

idioms.literal: I am glad to see you
I ask you to treat me well
idioms.meaning: please look after me / I look forward to it
it is fine / I am okay

mistakes.why: 입니다 already ends the sentence — 있어요 does not follow it.
반갑습니다 is the whole greeting; stacking another thanks sounds mechanical.
미나 ends in a vowel: 예요. 이에요 follows a consonant, as in 학생이에요.

task.title: Introduce yourself in five sentences
task.instructions: Write five Korean sentences: your name with 입니다, where you live with 에 살아요, what you study or do, one thing you drink or eat, and one closing hello. Read them aloud twice — 아요/어요 endings should sound like one word, not two.
